title: Καλυψοῦς ὅρκος
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Hermes delivers Zeus's command: the man Calypso keeps, the most wretched of all who fought at Troy, must be sent home without delay, since it is not his lot to die far from his own people. Calypso answers with a bitter complaint that the gods begrudge goddesses their mortal lovers, as they did when Dawn took Orion and Demeter lay with Iasion; yet she yields, though she has no ship or crew to send him with. Hermes warns her not to provoke Zeus's anger and departs. Calypso finds Odysseus weeping on the shore, where he spends his days longing for home, and tells him to build a raft, promising food, clothing and a fair wind. Odysseus shudders, suspecting a trap, and will not board it unless she swears a great oath; she smiles, calls him a rogue, and swears by earth, sky and the water of the Styx that she means him no harm.

sentences.t: εἰρωτᾷς μ’ ἐλθόντα θεὰ θεόν·
sentences.tr: eirōtāis m’ elthonta thea theon·
sentences.l: “You ask me, goddess, a god, about my coming;
sentences.i: “You, a goddess, ask me, a god, why I have come.
sentences.n: εἰρωτᾷς is the epic form of ἐρωτάω ‘ask’, with the stem lengthened to εἰ-. μ’ ἐλθόντα is ‘me, having come’: the participle carries the question, ‘about my coming’. θεὰ θεόν sets the two words side by side. θεά may be taken as a vocative, ‘goddess’, or as a nominative in apposition to the subject, ‘you, a goddess’; either way one god is questioning another. Hermes is answering the question Calypso put to him before the meal.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγώ τοι
νημερτέως τὸν μῦθον ἐνισπήσω·
sentences.tr:
autar egō toi
nēmerteōs ton mython enispēsō·
sentences.l:
but I to you
unerringly will tell the word;
sentences.i: But I will tell you my message, and tell it unerringly;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is the epic ‘but, and then’. τοι is the enclitic dative ‘to you’ (Attic σοι). νημερτέως ‘unerringly’ is the adverb of νημερτής, the adjective already fixed as ‘unerring’, from νη- ‘not’ and the root of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss the mark’. ἐνισπήσω is a future of ἐνέπω, a by-form of ἐννέπω ‘tell’, the verb of the poem’s first line. τὸν μῦθον is ‘the word, the matter’ she asked about: μῦθος in Homer is any spoken word or message.

sentences.t: κέλεαι γάρ.
sentences.tr: keleai gar.
sentences.l: for you bid me.
sentences.i: since you bid me.
sentences.n: κέλεαι is the second singular present of κέλομαι ‘bid, urge’, left uncontracted (Attic would contract -εαι to -ῃ). γάρ gives the reason for the promise just made: Hermes will speak plainly because Calypso has asked him to. These two words fill out line 98 after the ano teleia at ἐνισπήσω, and the full stop after them closes his courteous preface before he names Zeus.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς ἐμέ γ’ ἠνώγει δεῦρ’ ἐλθέμεν οὐκ ἐθέλοντα·
sentences.tr: Zeus eme g’ ēnōgei deur’ elthemen ouk ethelonta·
sentences.l: Zeus bade me, me, come here, though I did not wish it;
sentences.i: It was Zeus who ordered me to come here, and I came unwillingly;
sentences.n: ἠνώγει is the pluperfect of ἄνωγα ‘command’, a perfect with present sense, so its pluperfect serves as a simple past, ‘bade’. γε stresses ἐμέ, ‘me’: Hermes is the one sent, and not by his own choice. ἐλθέμεν is an epic infinitive in -έμεν (Attic ἐλθεῖν). οὐκ ἐθέλοντα agrees with ἐμέ, ‘not wishing it’. Hermes insists that the errand is Zeus’s and not his own, and so stands apart from the unwelcome message before he delivers it.

sentences.t:
τίς δ’ ἂν ἑκὼν τοσσόνδε διαδράμοι ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ
ἄσπετον;
sentences.tr:
tis d’ an hekōn tossonde diadramoi halmyron hydōr
aspeton;
sentences.l:
and who of his own will would race across so great a stretch of briny water,
beyond telling?
sentences.i: who would willingly race across such a vast stretch of salt water, more than words can tell?
sentences.n: τίς … ἂν … διαδράμοι is a potential optative in a question, ‘who would run across?’, expecting the answer ‘no one’. διαδράμοι is the aorist optative of διατρέχω, whose aorist is built on the root δραμ-. τοσσόνδε, with the epic double σ, is ‘so great a stretch’. ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ ‘briny water’ is the plain phrase for sea-water. ἄσπετον, held over to the start of line 101, is ‘unspeakable’, from ἀ- ‘not’ and the root of ἔννεπε ‘tell’: vast beyond telling.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις ἄγχι βροτῶν πόλις, οἵ τε θεοῖσιν
ἱερά τε ῥέζουσι καὶ ἐξαίτους ἑκατόμβας.
sentences.tr:
oude tis anchi brotōn polis, hoi te theoisin
hiera te rhezousi kai exaitous hekatombas.
sentences.l:
Nor is there near any city of mortals, who to the gods
both perform sacred-rites and picked-out hecatombs.
sentences.i: And there is no city of mortals near at hand, men who offer the gods sacrifices and choice hecatombs.
sentences.n: πόλις has no verb: supply ἐστί, ‘there is’. The relative οἵ is plural though πόλις is singular, because the sense passes to its people, βροτῶν; this is a construction according to sense. τε after οἵ is the epic τε of habitual action, ‘men who regularly offer’. ῥέζουσι ‘perform, offer’ takes both objects: ἱερά ‘sacred things, offerings’ and ἐξαίτους ἑκατόμβας, hecatombs of ‘picked, choice’ beasts. Hermes complains as a god: no worshippers live near Calypso’s island, so a visiting god finds no sacrifice there.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ οὔ πως ἔστι Διὸς νόον αἰγιόχοιο
οὔτε παρεξελθεῖν ἄλλον θεὸν οὔθ’ ἁλιῶσαι.
sentences.tr:
alla mal’ ou pōs esti Dios noon aigiochoio
oute parexelthein allon theon outh’ haliōsai.
sentences.l:
But there is no way at all that the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus
any other god should either slip past or bring to nothing.
sentences.i: But there is no way at all for any other god to slip past the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus or bring it to nothing.
sentences.n: οὔ πως ἔστι, with ἔστι accented on its first syllable, is ‘it is in no way possible’. The accusative Διὸς νόον αἰγιόχοιο is the object of both infinitives, and ἄλλον θεόν is their subject. παρεξελθεῖν, with two preverbs, is ‘to get past, evade’. ἁλιῶσαι, from ἁλιόω, is ‘to make vain, frustrate’ (compare ἅλιος ‘fruitless’). αἰγιόχοιο ‘aegis-bearing’ has a disputed sense and keeps the table’s wording. Calypso repeats these two lines at 5.137–138 with only the opening words changed.

sentences.t:
φησί τοι ἄνδρα παρεῖναι ὀιζυρώτατον ἄλλων,
τῶν ἀνδρῶν, οἳ ἄστυ πέρι Πριάμοιο μάχοντο
εἰνάετες, δεκάτῳ δὲ πόλιν πέρσαντες ἔβησαν
οἴκαδ’·
sentences.tr:
phēsi toi andra pareinai oizyrōtaton allōn,
tōn andrōn, hoi asty peri Priamoio machonto
einaetes, dekatōi de polin persantes ebēsan
oikad’·
sentences.l:
He says that there is with you a man most wretched beyond the others,
beyond those men who around the city of Priam fought
nine years, and in the tenth, having sacked the city, set off
homeward;
sentences.i: He says that you have with you a man more wretched than all the others who fought around the city of Priam for nine years, and in the tenth year sacked it and set off for home;
sentences.n: φησί ‘he says’ has Zeus as its subject, carried over from line 99. παρεῖναι, from πάρειμι, is ‘to be present, to be with (you)’. ὀιζυρώτατον ἄλλων mixes a superlative with a genitive of comparison, ‘most wretched beyond the others’, and τῶν ἀνδρῶν then says which others. ἄστυ πέρι is ‘around the city’, the preposition placed after its noun with its accent drawn back (anastrophe). μάχοντο is an unaugmented imperfect. εἰνάετες ‘for nine years’ is built on εἰνα-, the epic by-form of ἐννέα. οἴκαδ’ ‘homeward’ runs over into line 108.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ ἐν νόστῳ Ἀθηναίην ἀλίτοντο,
ἥ σφιν ἐπῶρσ’ ἄνεμόν τε κακὸν καὶ κύματα μακρά.
sentences.tr:
atar en nostōi Athēnaiēn alitonto,
hē sphin epōrs’ anemon te kakon kai kymata makra.
sentences.l:
but on their homecoming they sinned against Athena,
who roused upon them an evil wind and long waves.
sentences.i: but on the way home they offended Athena, who raised an evil wind and long waves against them.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is a by-form of αὐτάρ, ‘but’. ἀλίτοντο is the aorist middle of ἀλιταίνω ‘sin against, offend’, and takes Ἀθηναίην as its direct object; the same root returns in Calypso’s teasing ἀλιτρός at 5.182. ἐπῶρσ’ is ἐπῶρσε, the augmented aorist of ἐπόρνυμι ‘rouse against’, with σφιν ‘against them’. The offence is not named. Hermes compresses the story: the storm Athena sent on the returning Achaeans explains how Odysseus came here, while Calypso at 5.130–132 gives the wreck to Zeus’s thunderbolt.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι μὲν πάντες ἀπέφθιθεν ἐσθλοὶ ἑταῖροι,
τὸν δ’ ἄρα δεῦρ’ ἄνεμός τε φέρων καὶ κῦμα πέλασσε.
sentences.tr:
enth’ alloi men pantes apephthithen esthloi hetairoi,
ton d’ ara deur’ anemos te pherōn kai kyma pelasse.
sentences.l:
There all the others perished, his good companions,
but him, then, the wind, bearing him, and the wave brought near to here.
sentences.i: There all his other good companions perished, but the wind and the wave carried him and brought him here.
sentences.n: ἀπέφθιθεν is a third plural aorist passive with the short epic ending -θεν for -θησαν (Attic ἀπεφθίθησαν), from ἀποφθίνω ‘perish’. ἐσθλοὶ ἑταῖροι ‘good companions’ stands in apposition at the end of the line: ‘all the others, his good companions’. τόν is the pronoun ‘him’. ἄνεμος and κῦμα, joined by τε … καί, take the singular verb πέλασσε ‘brought near’, from πελάζω; the participle φέρων goes with ἄνεμος. Calypso speaks these two lines again, word for word, at 5.133–134.

sentences.t: τὸν νῦν σ’ ἠνώγειν ἀποπεμπέμεν ὅττι τάχιστα·
sentences.tr: ton nyn s’ ēnōgein apopempemen hotti tachista·
sentences.l: Him now he bade you send away with all speed;
sentences.i: He bade you send this man away now, with all speed;
sentences.n: ἠνώγειν is a third singular pluperfect in -ειν, an epic variant of the -ει seen in ἠνώγει at line 99; again it serves as a simple past, ‘he bade’, with Zeus as subject. σ’ is σε, ‘you’, the one commanded. ἀποπεμπέμεν is an epic infinitive in -έμεν, ‘to send away’. ὅττι τάχιστα, with the epic double τ, is Attic ὅτι τάχιστα ‘as quickly as possible’. τὸν νῦν puts ‘him’ first: the man just described is what the order is about.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ οἱ τῇδ’ αἶσα φίλων ἀπονόσφιν ὀλέσθαι,
ἀλλ’ ἔτι οἱ μοῖρ’ ἐστὶ φίλους τ’ ἰδέειν καὶ ἱκέσθαι
οἶκον ἐς ὑψόροφον καὶ ἑὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.tr:
ou gar hoi tēid’ aisa philōn aponosphin olesthai,
all’ eti hoi moir’ esti philous t’ ideein kai hikesthai
oikon es hypsorophon kai heēn es patrida gaian.
sentences.i: for it is not his lot to perish here, far from his dear ones; it is still his fate to see his dear ones again, and reach his high-roofed home and his own fatherland.”
sentences.n: αἶσα and μοῖρα are both a ‘share, lot’: what falls to a man as his portion. τῇδ’ is ‘here’. φίλων ἀπονόσφιν is ‘far from his dear ones’, the preposition following its genitive. ἰδέειν is the uncontracted aorist infinitive (Attic ἰδεῖν). The last line already stood in Zeus’s own instructions, at 5.42, and its English is kept, closing quotation mark and all; the line before varies Zeus’s ὣς γάρ ‘for so’ with ἀλλ’ ἔτι ‘but still’. Hermes ends his message in Zeus’s words.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, ῥίγησεν δὲ Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων,
καί μιν φωνήσασ’ ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, rhigēsen de Kalypsō, dia theaōn,
kai min phōnēsas’ epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and shuddered, Calypso, heavenly-one of goddesses,
and, lifting her voice, to him winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Calypso, heavenly even among goddesses, shuddered, and, raising her voice, spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: ῥίγησεν is the aorist of ῥιγέω ‘shudder, shiver’, from the root of ῥῖγος ‘cold, frost’: it names a bodily chill of dread, not mere surprise. The same frame recurs at 5.171, when Odysseus hears Calypso’s offer. δῖα θεάων keeps its fixed rendering. The second line already stands in an earlier part, of Athena, and its English is kept. φωνήσασ’ is φωνήσασα ‘having raised her voice’, μιν is ‘him’, Hermes, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the standing formula of address.

sentences.t:
σχέτλιοί ἐστε, θεοί, ζηλήμονες ἔξοχον ἄλλων,
οἵ τε θεαῖς ἀγάασθε παρ’ ἀνδράσιν εὐνάζεσθαι
ἀμφαδίην, ἤν τίς τε φίλον ποιήσετ’ ἀκοίτην.
sentences.tr:
schetlioi este, theoi, zēlēmones exochon allōn,
hoi te theais agaasthe par’ andrasin eunazesthai
amphadiēn, ēn tis te philon poiēset’ akoitēn.
sentences.l:
“Cruel you are, you gods, jealous beyond all others,
you who begrudge goddesses that beside men they should lie
openly, if one makes a man her dear bedfellow.
sentences.i: “You are cruel, you gods, and jealous beyond all others, you who resent it when goddesses openly lie beside men, if one of them makes a man her own dear bedfellow.
sentences.n: σχέτλιοι ‘cruel, hard-hearted’ is a word of reproach. ζηλήμονες ‘jealous’ is built on ζῆλος; ἔξοχον ἄλλων is ‘beyond all others’. ἀγάασθε, with the vowel stretched (diectasis), is from ἄγαμαι, which means ‘wonder at’ and then ‘resent, begrudge’; it takes the infinitive εὐνάζεσθαι ‘to lie, to go to bed’. ἀμφαδίην is ‘openly’. ἤν is the epic form of ἐάν, and ποιήσετ’ is an aorist subjunctive with short vowel (Attic ποιήσηται). ἀκοίτην ‘bedfellow, husband’ is from copulative ἀ- and κοίτη ‘bed’.

sentences.t:
ὣς μὲν ὅτ’ Ὠρίων’ ἕλετο ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
τόφρα οἱ ἠγάασθε θεοὶ ῥεῖα ζώοντες,
ἧος ἐν Ὀρτυγίῃ χρυσόθρονος Ἄρτεμις ἁγνὴ
οἷς ἀγανοῖς βελέεσσιν ἐποιχομένη κατέπεφνεν.
sentences.tr:
hōs men hot’ Ōriōn’ heleto rhododaktylos Ēōs,
tophra hoi ēgaasthe theoi rheia zōontes,
hēos en Ortygiēi chrysothronos Artemis hagnē
hois aganois beleessin epoichomenē katepephnen.
sentences.l:
So, when Orion she took for her own, rose-fingered Dawn,
all that while you begrudged her, you gods who live at ease,
until in Ortygia golden-throned Artemis the pure
with her gentle shafts assailing slew him.
sentences.i: So it was when rose-fingered Dawn took Orion for her own: all that while you gods who live at ease begrudged her, until golden-throned Artemis the pure came upon him in Ortygia with her gentle arrows and killed him.
sentences.n: ὥς ‘so’ opens Calypso’s first example, and ὣς δ’ (125) and ὣς δ’ αὖ νῦν (129) answer it: two precedents, then her own case. ἕλετο, aorist middle of αἱρέω, is ‘took for herself’; οἱ is ‘her’, Dawn. θεοὶ ῥεῖα ζώοντες keeps the wording already shipped, ‘the gods who live at ease’. ἧος is the epic form of Attic ἕως ‘until’. Ortygia, ‘Quail-island’, cannot be located with certainty. χρυσόθρονος is ‘golden-throned’, though an old alternative derives it from θρόνα ‘embroidered flowers’. Artemis’s ‘gentle shafts’ bring sudden, painless death.

sentences.t:
ὣς δ’ ὁπότ’ Ἰασίωνι ἐυπλόκαμος Δημήτηρ,
ᾧ θυμῷ εἴξασα, μίγη φιλότητι καὶ εὐνῇ
νειῷ ἔνι τριπόλῳ·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hopot’ Iasiōni eyplokamos Dēmētēr,
hōi thymōi eixasa, migē philotēti kai eunēi
neiōi eni tripolōi·
sentences.i: And so it was when fine-plaited Demeter, yielding to her own heart, lay in love with Iasion in a thrice-ploughed fallow field;
sentences.n: ὁπότ’ is ὁπότε ‘when’. Ἰασίωνι is dative with μίγη, the unaugmented aorist passive of μίγνυμι ‘mix, mingle’, the regular Homeric word for sexual union, here with φιλότητι καὶ εὐνῇ ‘in love and in bed’. ᾧ θυμῷ is the possessive ‘her own heart’, dative with εἴξασα, the aorist participle of εἴκω ‘yield’. ἐυπλόκαμος ‘fine-plaited’, Calypso’s own epithet in the part before, is given to Demeter here. νειῷ ἔνι τριπόλῳ, with ἔνι after its noun, is ‘in a fallow field turned three times by the plough’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ δὴν ἦεν ἄπυστος
Ζεύς, ὅς μιν κατέπεφνε βαλὼν ἀργῆτι κεραυνῷ.
sentences.tr:
oude dēn ēen apystos
Zeus, hos min katepephne balōn argēti keraunōi.
sentences.l:
nor long was he without tidings of it,
Zeus, who slew him, striking him with the bright thunderbolt.
sentences.i: and Zeus was not long in hearing of it; he struck Iasion with the bright thunderbolt and killed him.
sentences.n: ἦεν is epic for ἦν. ἄπυστος ‘without tidings, unaware’ is from ἀ- ‘not’ and the root of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn by hearsay’; the litotes ‘not long without tidings’ means that Zeus soon heard. μιν is ‘him’, Iasion. κατέπεφνε is the reduplicated aorist ‘slew’, the same form used of Artemis at line 124. βαλών is ‘striking’. ἀργῆτι is the dative of ἀργής ‘bright, vivid white’, of the lightning-flash: the same root ἀργ- as ἀργός, but a separate adjective.

sentences.t: ὣς δ’ αὖ νῦν μοι ἄγασθε, θεοί, βροτὸν ἄνδρα παρεῖναι.
sentences.tr: hōs d’ au nyn moi agasthe, theoi, broton andra pareinai.
sentences.l: So again now you begrudge me, gods, that a mortal man be beside me.
sentences.i: And so now, once again, you gods begrudge me the company of a mortal man.
sentences.n: ἄγασθε is the plain present of ἄγαμαι, beside the stretched ἀγάασθε of line 119 and the imperfect ἠγάασθε of line 122: the verb of resentment runs through the whole speech. μοι is ‘me’, the one begrudged, and θεοί is a vocative. βροτὸν ἄνδρα παρεῖναι ‘that a mortal man is at my side’ picks up Hermes’s own ἄνδρα παρεῖναι of line 105 and turns it back on the gods. αὖ νῦν ‘now again’ sets her case beside the two precedents.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼν ἐσάωσα περὶ τρόπιος βεβαῶτα
οἶον, ἐπεί οἱ νῆα θοὴν ἀργῆτι κεραυνῷ
Ζεὺς ἔλσας ἐκέασσε μέσῳ ἐνὶ οἴνοπι πόντῳ.
sentences.tr:
ton men egōn esaōsa peri tropios bebaōta
oion, epei hoi nēa thoēn argēti keraunōi
Zeus elsas ekeasse mesōi eni oinopi pontōi.
sentences.l:
Him it was I who saved, as he bestrode the keel,
alone, when his swift ship, with the bright thunderbolt,
Zeus, having pinned it, shattered in the middle of the wine-faced open-sea.
sentences.i: It was I who saved him, as he sat astride the keel all alone, after Zeus had pinned down his swift ship with the bright thunderbolt and shattered it in the middle of the sea that has the look of wine.
sentences.n: ἐγών is a form of ἐγώ used before a vowel. ἐσάωσα is the aorist of σαόω ‘save’ (Attic σῴζω). περὶ τρόπιος βεβαῶτα is ‘having gone astride the keel’: βεβαῶτα is the perfect participle of βαίνω, and περί with the genitive pictures his legs round the beam. οἶον ‘alone’ runs over into line 131. ἔλσας is the aorist participle of εἴλω ‘hem in, pin down’; ἐκέασσε is the aorist of κεάζω ‘split’. οἴνοπι πόντῳ keeps its fixed rendering. Here the wreck is Zeus’s work, not Athena’s storm.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι μὲν πάντες ἀπέφθιθεν ἐσθλοὶ ἑταῖροι,
τὸν δ’ ἄρα δεῦρ’ ἄνεμός τε φέρων καὶ κῦμα πέλασσε.
sentences.tr:
enth’ alloi men pantes apephthithen esthloi hetairoi,
ton d’ ara deur’ anemos te pherōn kai kyma pelasse.
sentences.l:
There all the others perished, his good companions,
but him, then, the wind, bearing him, and the wave brought near to here.
sentences.i: There all his other good companions perished, but the wind and the wave carried him and brought him here.
sentences.n: These two lines repeat 5.110–111 word for word, and their English is kept. Hermes spoke them in his report of Zeus’s account; Calypso now speaks them of the man she herself rescued, and in her version the ship went down under Zeus’s thunderbolt (line 131), not in Athena’s storm. ἀπέφθιθεν is again the short epic aorist passive, ‘perished’. δεῦρο ‘here’ is now her own island, where she is speaking. τὸν μέν opens the lines on either side, 130 and 135.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ φίλεόν τε καὶ ἔτρεφον, ἠδὲ ἔφασκον
θήσειν ἀθάνατον καὶ ἀγήραον ἤματα πάντα.
sentences.tr:
ton men egō phileon te kai etrephon, ēde ephaskon
thēsein athanaton kai agēraon ēmata panta.
sentences.l:
Him I both loved and nurtured, and I kept saying
I would make him immortal and ageless all his days.
sentences.i: I loved him and nurtured him, and I kept telling him I would make him immortal and ageless for all his days.
sentences.n: φίλεον is an unaugmented, uncontracted imperfect (Attic ἐφίλουν), and ἔτρεφον ‘fed, nurtured’ is imperfect too: continuing care. ἔφασκον is an iterative in -σκ-, ‘I kept saying’. θήσειν is the future infinitive of τίθημι, here ‘make’ with two predicate adjectives, ἀθάνατον ‘immortal’ and ἀγήραον ‘ageless’, from ἀ- ‘not’ and γῆρας ‘old age’. ἤματα πάντα keeps its fixed ‘all his days’. The two lines report Calypso’s offer; lines 151–158 show how Odysseus spent his days with her.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ οὔ πως ἔστι Διὸς νόον αἰγιόχοιο
οὔτε παρεξελθεῖν ἄλλον θεὸν οὔθ’ ἁλιῶσαι,
ἐρρέτω, εἴ μιν κεῖνος ἐποτρύνει καὶ ἀνώγει,
πόντον ἐπ’ ἀτρύγετον·
sentences.tr:
all’ epei ou pōs esti Dios noon aigiochoio
oute parexelthein allon theon outh’ haliōsai,
erretō, ei min keinos epotrynei kai anōgei,
ponton ep’ atrygeton·
sentences.i: But since there is no way for any other god to slip past the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus or bring it to nothing, let him go to ruin, if that god urges him on and commands it, over the sea that yields no harvest;
sentences.n: The first two lines repeat Hermes’s lines 103–104 with ἀλλ’ ἐπεί ‘but since’ in place of ἀλλὰ μάλ’, and their English is kept. ἐρρέτω is the third singular imperative of ἔρρω ‘go to one’s ruin, be gone’: a curse. κεῖνος ‘that one’ is Zeus, held at arm’s length. ἐποτρύνει καὶ ἀνώγει pairs two verbs of command; ἀνώγει is here a present, formed from the perfect ἄνωγα. πόντον ἐπ’ ἀτρύγετον ‘over the unharvested sea’ finishes the curse; the meaning of ἀτρύγετος is unknown, and ‘unharvested’ is the house guess.

sentences.t: πέμψω δέ μιν οὔ πῃ ἐγώ γε·
sentences.tr: pempsō de min ou pēi egō ge·
sentences.l: but I will not send him anywhere, not I;
sentences.i: but I, for my part, will not send him anywhere;
sentences.n: πέμψω is future. πέμπω here means ‘send home’ in the full sense: a host sends a departing guest with a ship and a crew. πῃ is ‘anywhere, in any way’. ἐγώ γε ‘I, at least’ sets her against Zeus: he may order the release, but she will not provide the voyage. The next line gives her reason, and the lines after it (143–144) say what she offers instead: not conveyance, but counsel.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ μοι πάρα νῆες ἐπήρετμοι καὶ ἑταῖροι,
οἵ κέν μιν πέμποιεν ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
ou gar moi para nēes epēretmoi kai hetairoi,
hoi ken min pempoien ep’ eurea nōta thalassēs.
sentences.l:
for I have no oared ships nor companions,
who might send him over the broad back of the sea.
sentences.i: for I have no oared ships or companions who might convey him over the sea's broad back.
sentences.n: The second line already stands in two earlier parts, in Proteus’s words as Menelaus reported them and in Athena’s plea, both of Odysseus held on this island; its English is kept. The first line differs from those only in μοι ‘to me’ for οἱ ‘to him’, and the English changes only there. πάρα, with its accent drawn back, stands for πάρεστι ‘are at hand’. ἐπήρετμοι is ‘fitted with oars’. οἵ κεν … πέμποιεν is a relative clause with the potential optative, ‘who might send him’.

sentences.t:
αὐτάρ οἱ πρόφρων ὑποθήσομαι, οὐδ’ ἐπικεύσω,
ὥς κε μάλ’ ἀσκηθὴς ἣν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἵκηται.
sentences.tr:
autar hoi prophrōn hypothēsomai, oud’ epikeusō,
hōs ke mal’ askēthēs hēn patrida gaian hikētai.
sentences.l:
But to him, ready-minded, I will give counsel, nor keep anything back,
so that quite unharmed he may reach his own fatherland.”
sentences.i: But I will give him counsel with a ready mind, and keep nothing back, so that he may reach his own fatherland quite unharmed.”
sentences.n: πρόφρων ‘ready-minded, willing’ is an adjective used of Calypso herself, where English wants an adverb, ‘with a ready mind’. ὑποθήσομαι is the future of ὑποτίθεμαι ‘give counsel’. οὐδ’ ἐπικεύσω is ‘nor will I keep anything back’. The second line already stood in Zeus’s instructions about Telemachus, and its English is kept. ἀσκηθής is ‘unharmed’, and μάλ’ strengthens it, ‘quite’. ἥν is the possessive ‘his own’. ἵκηται is the aorist subjunctive in the purpose clause with κε.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe diaktoros argeïphontēs·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed the guide, Argeïphontes:
sentences.i: Then the guide, the slayer of Argus, spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: This is the fixed reply-formula τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε ‘Him then in turn addressed’, here with τήν ‘her’, Calypso, and the speaker named at the end of the line. διάκτορος ‘the guide’ and ἀργεϊφόντης ‘Argeïphontes’ are both standing epithets of Hermes, and neither is understood. διάκτορος may mean ‘guide’ or ‘messenger’. ἀργεϊφόντης was read in antiquity as ‘slayer of Argus’, which the i layer follows, but other explanations were offered.

sentences.t:
οὕτω νῦν ἀπόπεμπε, Διὸς δ’ ἐποπίζεο μῆνιν,
μή πώς τοι μετόπισθε κοτεσσάμενος χαλεπήνῃ.
sentences.tr:
houtō nyn apopempe, Dios d’ epopizeo mēnin,
mē pōs toi metopisthe kotessamenos chalepēnēi.
sentences.l:
“So now send him away, and beware the wrath of Zeus,
lest somehow hereafter, bearing a grudge, he be harsh with you.”
sentences.i: “Then send him away now, just so, and beware the wrath of Zeus, or he may bear you a grudge hereafter and deal harshly with you.”
sentences.n: οὕτω ‘so’, with ἀπόπεμπε, the present imperative ‘send away’, holds Calypso to what she has just said. ἐποπίζεο is the uncontracted present imperative middle of ἐποπίζομαι ‘regard with awe, respect’, built on ὄπις, the watchful regard of the gods. μῆνις is the lasting wrath of a god. μή with the subjunctive χαλεπήνῃ is a clause of fear, ‘lest he be harsh’. κοτεσσάμενος is the aorist participle of κοτέω ‘bear a grudge’, and μετόπισθε is ‘hereafter’. Hermes answers none of her complaint.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη κρατὺς ἀργεϊφόντης·
sentences.tr: hōs ara phōnēsas apebē kratys argeïphontēs·
sentences.l: So then having spoken, away he went, the strong Argeïphontes;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the strong slayer of Argus went off;
sentences.n: This is the masculine closing formula ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη ‘So then having spoken, away he went’, filled out with κρατὺς ἀργεϊφόντης ‘the strong Argeïphontes’, as in the part before. κρατύς ‘strong, mighty’ is a plain adjective on κράτος ‘strength’. ἀπέβη is the augmented aorist of ἀποβαίνω. The paragraph mark at this line begins a new stretch of narrative: the god leaves, and the story follows Calypso to the shore.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἐπ’ Ὀδυσσῆα μεγαλήτορα πότνια νύμφη
ἤι’, ἐπεὶ δὴ Ζηνὸς ἐπέκλυεν ἀγγελιάων.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ep’ Odyssēa megalētora potnia nymphē
ēi’, epei dē Zēnos epeklyen angeliaōn.
sentences.l:
And she, to great-spirited Odysseus, the lady nymph,
went, since indeed she had heard the messages of Zeus.
sentences.i: And the lady nymph went to find great-spirited Odysseus, now that she had heard the message of Zeus.
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’, the pronoun. πότνια ‘lady’ is a title of respect, given to Calypso at 1.14, and νύμφη is her kind, a goddess of place. ἤι’ is ἤιε, the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, elided and held over to the start of line 150. ἐπέκλυεν, from ἐπικλύω, takes the genitive of what is heard: Ζηνὸς … ἀγγελιάων ‘the messages of Zeus’, with Ζηνός, the second genitive stem of Ζεύς, and a genitive plural in -άων (Attic -ῶν). μεγαλήτορα keeps its fixed ‘great-spirited’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ ἀκτῆς εὗρε καθήμενον·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ar’ ep’ aktēs heure kathēmenon·
sentences.l: And him then on the shore she found, sitting;
sentences.i: She found him sitting on the shore;
sentences.n: εὗρε is the aorist of εὑρίσκω ‘find’. καθήμενον, the present participle of κάθημαι ‘sit’, gives the state she found him in, the same posture described when Hermes arrived (κλαῖε καθήμενος, 5.82). ἐπ’ ἀκτῆς, with the genitive, is ‘on the shore’. ἄρ’ is ἄρα, ‘then, as it proved’. The short clause ends at an ano teleia in the middle of line 151, and the rest of the line opens an account of how he spent his nights and days.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ ποτ’ ὄσσε
δακρυόφιν τέρσοντο, κατείβετο δὲ γλυκὺς αἰὼν
νόστον ὀδυρομένῳ, ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι ἥνδανε νύμφη.
sentences.tr:
oude pot’ osse
dakryophin tersonto, kateibeto de glykys aiōn
noston odyromenōi, epei ouketi hēndane nymphē.
sentences.l:
nor ever were his eyes
dry of tears, and his sweet life was ebbing away
as he lamented his homecoming, since the nymph no longer pleased him.
sentences.i: his eyes were never dry of tears, and his sweet life was ebbing away as he mourned for his homecoming, since the nymph no longer pleased him.
sentences.n: ὄσσε is a dual, ‘his two eyes’, with a plural verb. δακρυόφιν has the suffix -φι(ν), here marking separation: ‘dry of tears’. τέρσοντο is the unaugmented imperfect of τέρσομαι ‘become dry’. κατείβετο, imperfect middle of κατείβω ‘let flow down’, is ‘was flowing away’; its participle κατειβόμενον returns for the Styx at line 185. γλυκὺς αἰών is ‘sweet life’. ὀδυρομένῳ is dative, ‘for him as he lamented’. ἥνδανε is the augmented imperfect of ἁνδάνω ‘please’, with νύμφη as subject.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι νύκτας μὲν ἰαύεσκεν καὶ ἀνάγκῃ
ἐν σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσι παρ’ οὐκ ἐθέλων ἐθελούσῃ·
sentences.tr:
all’ ē toi nyktas men iauesken kai anankēi
en spessi glaphyroisi par’ ouk ethelōn ethelousēi·
sentences.l:
But truly, by night he would sleep, even under constraint,
in the hollow caves, unwilling, beside her who was willing;
sentences.i: True, at night he would sleep beside her in the hollow caves, because he had to, he unwilling and she willing;
sentences.n: ἦ τοι ‘truly, to be sure’ concedes a point before δ’ in line 156 answers it: nights with her, days on the shore. νύκτας is an accusative of time, ‘through the nights’. ἰαύεσκεν is an iterative imperfect in -σκ- of ἰαύω ‘sleep, pass the night’. ἀνάγκῃ ‘under constraint’ is the word of Athena’s complaint at 5.14. ἐν σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσι keeps its fixed ‘in hollow caves’. παρ’ goes with ἐθελούσῃ, ‘beside her who was willing’, and οὐκ ἐθέλων ἐθελούσῃ sets his participle against hers.

sentences.t:
ἤματα δ’ ἂμ πέτρῃσι καὶ ἠιόνεσσι καθίζων
δάκρυσι καὶ στοναχῇσι καὶ ἄλγεσι θυμὸν ἐρέχθων
πόντον ἐπ’ ἀτρύγετον δερκέσκετο δάκρυα λείβων.
sentences.tr:
ēmata d’ am petrēisi kai ēionessi kathizōn
dakrysi kai stonachēisi kai algesi thymon erechthōn
ponton ep’ atrygeton derkesketo dakrya leibōn.
sentences.l:
but by day, sitting on the rocks and the beaches,
racking his heart with tears and groans and pains,
toward the unharvested sea he kept gazing, tears pouring.
sentences.i: but by day he sat on the rocks and the beaches, tormenting his heart with tears and groans and pain, and kept gazing out over the sea that yields no harvest, pouring out his tears.
sentences.n: ἤματα, like νύκτας, is an accusative of time, ‘by day’. ἄμ is ἀνά cut short, its ν assimilated before π: ‘along, among’. ἠιόνεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι of ἠιών ‘beach’. The last two lines already stood in the part before, when Hermes found Odysseus in the same place, and their English is kept; only the punctuation changes, since here the lines continue one sentence: the full stop after ‘pains’ becomes a comma, and the capital that opened the next line is lowered. δερκέσκετο is an iterative imperfect, ‘kept gazing’.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη προσεφώνεε δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr: anchou d’ histamenē prosephōnee dia theaōn·
sentences.l: And standing close by, she spoke to him, heavenly-one of goddesses:
sentences.i: And she, heavenly even among goddesses, came and stood close beside him, and spoke to him:
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ is ‘near’, and ἱσταμένη, the present middle participle of ἵστημι, is ‘coming to stand’: she comes up and stands close beside him. προσεφώνεε is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’ (Attic προσεφώνει); ‘addressed’ is kept for προσέειπε. δῖα θεάων, standing alone as subject, keeps its fixed rendering. The ano teleia closes the introduction, and Murray begins a new paragraph with her speech.

sentences.t:
κάμμορε, μή μοι ἔτ’ ἐνθάδ’ ὀδύρεο, μηδέ τοι αἰὼν
φθινέτω·
sentences.tr:
kammore, mē moi et’ enthad’ odyreo, mēde toi aiōn
phthinetō·
sentences.l:
“Ill-fated one, do not, I pray, lament here any longer, nor let your life
waste away;
sentences.i: “Ill-fated man, do not go on lamenting here any longer, I pray you, and do not let your life waste away;
sentences.n: κάμμορε is κατάμορε, with κατά cut short and its τ assimilated to μ: ‘ill-fated’, one whose μόρος ‘portion’ is bad. μοι is an ethic dative, ‘for my sake, I pray’. ὀδύρεο is the uncontracted present imperative middle of ὀδύρομαι ‘lament’ (Attic ὀδύρου), after μή. φθινέτω is the third singular present imperative of φθίνω ‘waste away’. αἰών ‘life’ takes up the narrator’s γλυκὺς αἰών of line 152: what the narrator said of him, Calypso now says to him.

sentences.t: ἤδη γάρ σε μάλα πρόφρασσ’ ἀποπέμψω.
sentences.tr: ēdē gar se mala prophrass’ apopempsō.
sentences.l: for now, very ready-minded, I will send you away.
sentences.i: for now I will send you on your way, and with a very ready mind.
sentences.n: ἤδη is ‘now, at last’. πρόφρασσ’ is πρόφρασσα, the epic feminine of πρόφρων ‘ready-minded, willing’; at line 143 Calypso used πρόφρων itself of herself, since the adjective can serve both genders. μάλα strengthens it. ἀποπέμψω is future, ‘I will send you away’, the verb of Zeus’s order at line 112, ἀποπεμπέμεν. Calypso says nothing to Odysseus of that order: in her words the release is her own decision.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δούρατα μακρὰ ταμὼν ἁρμόζεο χαλκῷ
εὐρεῖαν σχεδίην·
sentences.tr:
all’ age dourata makra tamōn harmozeo chalkōi
eureian schediēn·
sentences.l:
But come, cutting long timbers, fit together with the bronze
a broad raft;
sentences.i: But come, cut long timbers with the bronze and fit them together into a broad raft;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε ‘but come’ urges, before an imperative. δούρατα is a plural of δόρυ, here ‘timbers, beams’ rather than ‘spears’. ταμών is the aorist participle of τέμνω ‘cut’. ἁρμόζεο is the uncontracted present imperative middle of ἁρμόζω ‘fit together’ (Attic ἁρμόζου), ‘fit together for yourself’. χαλκῷ ‘with the bronze’ means a bronze tool, axe or adze. σχεδίη ‘raft’ is the vessel Zeus named at 5.33; εὐρεῖαν ‘broad’ opens line 163.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ ἴκρια πῆξαι ἐπ’ αὐτῆς
ὑψοῦ, ὥς σε φέρῃσιν ἐπ’ ἠεροειδέα πόντον.
sentences.tr:
atar ikria pēxai ep’ autēs
hypsou, hōs se pherēisin ep’ ēeroeidea ponton.
sentences.l:
and fix decking upon it
high up, so that it may carry you over the misty-looking sea.
sentences.i: and fasten a deck upon it, high up, so that it may carry you over the misty-looking sea.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘and, but’ carries on the instructions. πῆξαι, from πήγνυμι ‘fix, fasten’, is most simply an aorist infinitive used as an imperative, a common Homeric construction; the aorist middle imperative has the same form, which would match the middle ἁρμόζεο. ἴκρια are ‘deck-planks’, decking laid over the frame, and ὑψοῦ ‘high up’ raises it above the water. ἐπ’ αὐτῆς ‘upon it’ refers to the raft. φέρῃσιν is a present subjunctive with the epic ending -ῃσι, in a purpose clause with ὥς. ἐπ’ ἠεροειδέα πόντον keeps its fixed ‘over the misty-looking sea’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ σῖτον καὶ ὕδωρ καὶ οἶνον ἐρυθρὸν
ἐνθήσω μενοεικέ’, ἅ κέν τοι λιμὸν ἐρύκοι,
εἵματά τ’ ἀμφιέσω·
sentences.tr:
autar egō siton kai hydōr kai oinon erythron
enthēsō menoeike’, ha ken toi limon erykoi,
heimata t’ amphiesō·
sentences.i: And I will put aboard bread and water and red wine, all you could desire, to keep hunger from you, and I will clothe you;
sentences.n: ἐγώ is set against the σύ implied in her commands: he builds, she provisions. σῖτος is ‘grain, bread’, food in general. ἐνθήσω, future of ἐντίθημι, is ‘put in, stow aboard’. μενοεικέ’ is μενοεικέα, neuter plural, ‘satisfying, suited to the desire’, compounded of μένος and the root of ἔοικα ‘suit’; it goes with all three provisions. ἅ κεν … ἐρύκοι is a relative clause with the potential optative, ‘which would keep off hunger’. ἀμφιέσω is the future of ἀμφιέννυμι ‘clothe’, with εἵματα ‘clothes’.

sentences.t:
πέμψω δέ τοι οὖρον ὄπισθεν,
ὥς κε μάλ’ ἀσκηθὴς σὴν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἵκηαι,
αἴ κε θεοί γ’ ἐθέλωσι, τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν,
οἵ μευ φέρτεροί εἰσι νοῆσαί τε κρῆναί τε.
sentences.tr:
pempsō de toi ouron opisthen,
hōs ke mal’ askēthēs sēn patrida gaian hikēai,
ai ke theoi g’ ethelōsi, toi ouranon euryn echousin,
hoi meu pherteroi eisi noēsai te krēnai te.
sentences.l:
and I will send you a fair wind behind,
so that quite unharmed you may reach your own fatherland,
if the gods, at least, are willing, who hold the wide sky,
who are stronger than I both to devise and to accomplish.”
sentences.i: and I will send a fair wind behind you, so that you may reach your own fatherland quite unharmed, if the gods who hold the wide sky are willing, who are stronger than I am both in devising and in bringing to pass.”
sentences.n: οὖρον ὄπισθεν is ‘a fair wind from behind’. The second line varies a line spoken of Telemachus at 5.26 and of Odysseus at 5.144: σήν ‘your own’ replaces ἥν ‘his own’, and ἵκηαι, the uncontracted second singular aorist subjunctive (Attic ἵκῃ), replaces ἵκηται. τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν ‘who hold the wide sky’ has τοί as a relative. μευ is a genitive of comparison with φέρτεροι ‘stronger’. νοῆσαι and κρῆναι (Attic κρᾶναι, from κραίνω ‘accomplish’) are infinitives of respect.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, ῥίγησεν δὲ πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, rhigēsen de polytlas dios Odysseus,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and shuddered, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
and, lifting his voice, to her winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus shuddered, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:
sentences.n: This frame repeats that of 5.116–117 with the roles changed: Odysseus now shudders at Calypso’s words, as she shuddered at Hermes’s. πολύτλας ‘much-enduring’, from πολύ ‘much’ and the root of τλῆναι ‘endure, bear’, is new to the poem here; it is kept apart from ταλασίφρων ‘enduring-minded’, built on the same root. δῖος keeps its fixed ‘heavenly’. The second line already stood in an earlier part, and its English is kept. What makes him shudder is the offer itself, as the next lines explain.

sentences.t:
ἄλλο τι δὴ σύ, θεά, τόδε μήδεαι, οὐδέ τι πομπήν,
ἥ με κέλεαι σχεδίῃ περάαν μέγα λαῖτμα θαλάσσης,
δεινόν τ’ ἀργαλέον τε·
sentences.tr:
allo ti dē sy, thea, tode mēdeai, oude ti pompēn,
hē me keleai schediēi peraan mega laitma thalassēs,
deinon t’ argaleon te·
sentences.i: “Surely, goddess, you are planning something else in this, and not my escort home at all, when you bid me cross the great gulf of the sea on a raft, a dread and grievous thing;
sentences.n: ἄλλο τι … τόδε ‘something else in this’ is the object of μήδεαι, the uncontracted present middle second singular of μήδομαι ‘devise’ (Attic μήδῃ). οὐδέ τι πομπήν is ‘and not at all my convoy’: πομπή is the escort a host gives a guest who is leaving. ἥ, feminine, is ‘you who’, referring to θεά. σχεδίῃ is an instrumental dative, ‘on a raft’. περάαν is περᾶν with the vowel stretched. μέγα λαῖτμα θαλάσσης keeps its shipped ‘the great gulf of the sea’. δεινόν τ’ ἀργαλέον τε agree with λαῖτμα.

sentences.t:
τὸ δ’ οὐδ’ ἐπὶ νῆες ἐῖσαι
ὠκύποροι περόωσιν, ἀγαλλόμεναι Διὸς οὔρῳ.
sentences.tr:
to d’ oud’ epi nēes eisai
ōkyporoi peroōsin, agallomenai Dios ourōi.
sentences.l:
it not even well-balanced ships,
swift-faring, cross, exulting in the fair wind of Zeus.
sentences.i: not even well-balanced, swift-faring ships cross it, exulting in a fair wind from Zeus.
sentences.n: τό is ‘it’, the gulf of the sea. ἐπί is here an adverb, ‘over it’, or stands apart from περόωσιν by tmesis. περόωσιν is περῶσιν with the vowel stretched (diectasis). νῆες ἐῖσαι keeps the house ‘well-balanced ships’, though the sense of the adjective is uncertain. ὠκύποροι ‘swift-faring’ is built from ὠκύς ‘swift’ and πόρος ‘passage’. ἀγαλλόμεναι Διὸς οὔρῳ ‘exulting in the fair wind of Zeus’ pictures ships running before a favouring wind, which is Zeus’s to send.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἂν ἐγὼν ἀέκητι σέθεν σχεδίης ἐπιβαίην,
εἰ μή μοι τλαίης γε, θεά, μέγαν ὅρκον ὀμόσσαι
μή τί μοι αὐτῷ πῆμα κακὸν βουλευσέμεν ἄλλο.
sentences.tr:
oud’ an egōn aekēti sethen schediēs epibaiēn,
ei mē moi tlaiēs ge, thea, megan horkon omossai
mē ti moi autōi pēma kakon bouleusemen allo.
sentences.l:
Nor would I, against your will, set foot upon a raft,
unless you would bring yourself, goddess, to swear me a great oath
that you will not plan some other evil woe against me myself.”
sentences.i: Nor would I set foot on a raft against your will, unless you would bring yourself, goddess, to swear me a great oath that you will not plan some other evil woe against me.”
sentences.n: ἂν … ἐπιβαίην is a potential optative, ‘I would not set foot on’, with σχεδίης a genitive after ἐπιβαίνω. ἀέκητι σέθεν is ‘against your will’, σέθεν being an epic genitive of σύ. The phrase is hard here, since Calypso is urging him to go: it seems to mean ‘without your true goodwill’, that is, unless he can be sure she wishes him well. τλαίης is the aorist optative of τλῆναι ‘bring oneself to’, the root of πολύτλας at line 171. ὀμόσσαι, with epic σσ, is the aorist infinitive of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’. βουλευσέμεν is a future infinitive in -σέμεν, ‘that you will plan’, after the oath.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δὲ Καλυψὼ δῖα θεάων,
χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, meidēsen de Kalypsō dia theaōn,
cheiri te min katerexen epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomazen·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and smiled, Calypso, heavenly-one of goddesses,
and stroked him with her hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Calypso, heavenly even among goddesses, smiled, and stroked him with her hand, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: The frame of 5.116 and 5.171 returns with a third reaction: not a shudder but a smile. μείδησεν is the aorist of μειδάω ‘smile’. The second line already stood in an earlier part, of Menelaus, and its English is kept, except that ‘his hand’ becomes ‘her hand’; χειρί itself has no possessive. κατέρεξεν is the aorist of καταρρέζω ‘stroke, caress’. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν keeps its fixed English, with ἔκ standing apart from ὀνόμαζεν by tmesis.

sentences.t:
ἦ δὴ ἀλιτρός γ’ ἐσσὶ καὶ οὐκ ἀποφώλια εἰδώς,
οἷον δὴ τὸν μῦθον ἐπεφράσθης ἀγορεῦσαι.
sentences.tr:
ē dē alitros g’ essi kai ouk apophōlia eidōs,
hoion dē ton mython epephrasthēs agoreusai.
sentences.l:
“Truly you are a rogue, and no knower of empty things,
such is the word you have thought to utter.
sentences.i: “What a rogue you are, and nothing you know is empty, to think of saying such a thing!
sentences.n: ἀλιτρός ‘offender, rogue’ is built on the root of ἀλιταίνω ‘sin against’, seen in ἀλίτοντο at line 108; here the word teases. ἐσσί is the epic second singular of εἰμί. οὐκ ἀποφώλια εἰδώς is litotes, ‘knowing things not empty’, that is, shrewd; ἀποφώλια is taken as ‘empty, vain’, but its formation is obscure. οἷον … ἐπεφράσθης gives the ground for the exclamation, ‘seeing what a speech you have thought to make’; ἐπεφράσθης is the aorist, passive in form, of ἐπιφράζομαι ‘think of, devise’. ἀγορεῦσαι is ‘to speak’.

sentences.t:
ἴστω νῦν τόδε γαῖα καὶ οὐρανὸς εὐρὺς ὕπερθε
καὶ τὸ κατειβόμενον Στυγὸς ὕδωρ, ὅς τε μέγιστος
ὅρκος δεινότατός τε πέλει μακάρεσσι θεοῖσι,
μή τί τοι αὐτῷ πῆμα κακὸν βουλευσέμεν ἄλλο.
sentences.tr:
istō nyn tode gaia kai ouranos eurys hyperthe
kai to kateibomenon Stygos hydōr, hos te megistos
horkos deinotatos te pelei makaressi theoisi,
mē ti toi autōi pēma kakon bouleusemen allo.
sentences.l:
Let now the earth know this, and the wide sky above,
and the down-flowing water of the Styx, which is the greatest
oath and the most dread for the blessed gods,
that I will not plan some other evil woe against you yourself.
sentences.i: Now let the earth know this, and the wide sky above, and the down-flowing water of the Styx, which is the greatest and most dread oath for the blessed gods, that I will not plan some other evil woe against you.
sentences.n: ἴστω is the third singular imperative of οἶδα ‘let … know’: earth, sky and the Styx are called on as witnesses. τόδε ‘this’ points forward to the μή-clause of line 187. Στυγὸς ὕδωρ is ‘the water of the Styx’, and κατειβόμενον ‘down-flowing’ is the verb of line 152. ὅς is masculine, attracted to ὅρκος, ‘which is the greatest oath’. πέλει is an epic ‘is’. μακάρεσσι θεοῖσι is ‘for the blessed gods’. Line 187 answers Odysseus’s line 179, with τοι ‘to you’ in place of μοι ‘to me’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν νοέω καὶ φράσσομαι, ἅσσ’ ἂν ἐμοί περ
αὐτῇ μηδοίμην, ὅτε με χρειὼ τόσον ἵκοι·
sentences.tr:
alla ta men noeō kai phrassomai, hass’ an emoi per
autēi mēdoimēn, hote me chreiō toson hikoi·
sentences.l:
But I have in mind and will take thought for those things which for myself
I would devise, if need so great should come upon me;
sentences.i: No: I have in mind, and will take thought for, just what I would devise for myself, if so great a need should come upon me;
sentences.n: τὰ μέν is ‘those things’, the antecedent of ἅσσ’, which is ἅσσα, the epic form of Attic ἅττα ‘whatever things’. νοέω is ‘I have in mind’. φράσσομαι is most naturally a future of φράζομαι with epic σσ, ‘I will take thought’, though a short-vowel aorist subjunctive is also possible. μηδοίμην is an optative with ἄν, ‘I would devise’, the verb of Odysseus’s μήδεαι at line 173. ἐμοί περ αὐτῇ is ‘for my very self’, with περ intensive. ὅτε … ἵκοι, with the optative, is ‘if ever such need should come upon me’. χρειώ is ‘need, necessity’.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ ἐμοὶ νόος ἐστὶν ἐναίσιμος, οὐδέ μοι αὐτῇ
θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι σιδήρεος, ἀλλ’ ἐλεήμων.
sentences.tr:
kai gar emoi noos estin enaisimos, oude moi autēi
thymos eni stēthessi sidēreos, all’ eleēmōn.
sentences.l:
for I too have a mind that is fitting, nor in me myself
is the heart within my breast of iron, but pitying.”
sentences.i: for I too have a mind that is fitting, and the heart within my breast is not of iron, but full of pity.”
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ is ‘for indeed, for also’. ἐναίσιμος ‘fitting, right’ is built on αἶσα ‘due share’, the word Hermes used of Odysseus’s lot at line 113. ἐνί is ἐν. στήθεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, ‘in the breast’, plural for a single breast. σιδήρεος ‘of iron’ is the image of an unfeeling heart. ἐλεήμων ‘pitying, compassionate’ is from ἔλεος ‘pity’. θυμός is here ‘heart’, the seat of feeling. With this line Calypso’s oath and speech are complete.
